newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: GOVERNMENT UNDER FIRE OVER CRITIQUE OF PACIFIC POLITICIANS
The Federal government is continuing to face criticism over the release of a scathing official critique of South Pacific political figures.

Australian diplomats are moving to minimise the damage caused by the country by country review. There's already been an angry response to the report's contents. The Cook Islands claims the briefing paper is both unfair and inaccurate.
Nauru says it's nothing more than a gossip sheet.
And New Zealand's Prime Minister, Jim Bolger, says he wouldn't like to be in John Howard's shoes today.
The Federal Government continues to disocciate itself from the report, saying the views expressed about certain South Pacific Ministers do not reflect official policy.
Opposition Leader Kim Beazley, who's visiting London, says the Government must apologise for the blunder.
"These are the sorts of stumbles you get from a completely inept government," Mr Beazley said.
AUSTRALIA CRITICISED FOR DISCRIMINATION AGAINST WOMEN
The United Nations is expected to release a report this week critical of Australia's performance under the Convention for Discrimination Against Women.
Australia has failed to meet its reporting obligations to the committee that monitors the Convention.
Australia was to have submitted a written report to the committee monitoring women's human rights a year ago.
On Friday, it presented an oral submission which the committee felt did not provide the necessary detail.

For example, it wanted to know what impact the move to part-time employment was having on women, and whether the problem of violence toward Aboriginal women was being addressed. Committee member, Justice Sylvia Cartwight says the committee wants much more evaluation and assessment of programs that have been reduced or abandoned, and new programs that are being introduced in their place, to see which are more beneficial.
DOCTORS RENEW CALL FOR MORE HOSPITAL FUNDING
Doctors have renewed calls for more funds to be poured into public hospitals following the results of a survey showing almost half those questioned feel the hospitals are failing.
The survey, commissioned by the Australian Medical Association, found that 42.5 per cent of people believe their local hospital is failing to provide efficient and effective service.

Of those, 43.5 per cent said current services were unable to meet the demand for them. Chairman of the AMA's Council of General Practice, Dr Joe Kosterich, says the Government has got to listen to criticism of funding levels.
Dr Kosterich says the survey is a damning indictment on the funding for public hospitals in Australia.

He says there's a lot of buck passing between the states and the Federal Government about who's supposed to pay, and "bean counters" in Canberra are fixed on 8.5 percent of GDP as the amount that should be spent on health.
But Dr Kosterich says the public of Australia are clearly saying they feel more money should be spent on health.
HEARINGS START OVER KIMBERLEY NATIVE TITLE CLAIM
Hearings have started in the Federal Court on a native title claim over large tracts of land in Western Australia's Kimberley region.

The claim covers more than 6,300 square kilometres of land and water in and around Kununurra and Wyndham, including Lake Argyle and Lake Kununurra, and parts of the Keep River National Park in the Northern Territory.

The Miriuwung and Gagerrong Peoples of Kununurra lodged the claim in 1994 and it was referred to the Federal Court by the National Native Title Tribunal because mediation between the parties failed to settle the matter.
About 400 parties including local Aborigines, farmers, mining companies, pastoralists, and the West Australian and Northern Territory Governments are expected to give evidence.
Two months have been set down for the hearings.
STONE SEEKS SUPPORT FOR RAILWAY LAND ACQUISITION
Northern Territory Chief Minister Shane Stone will seek legislative support from the Commonwealth for the Alice Springs to Darwin railway.

Mr Stone said the Territory did not have the power to acquire Aboriginal land for the railway corridor. He wants the Prime Minister to intervene, either by acquiring the land or giving the Territory Government the power to do so.
"There are aspects of the corridor that are affected by land rights and by native title," Mr Stone said.
Mr Stone and South Australian Premier John Olsen will meet the Prime Minister on Thursday.
CLOTHING MAKER SIGNS OUTWORKER CODE
Unions say clothing manufacturer, Sportsgirl-Sportscraft, has had a major turnaround in their attitude to outworkers.

The ACTU is claiming victory following a last minute signing of a work code of practice. The Fair Wear campaign comprising unions, church and community groups has for several months, targetted manufacturers like Sportsgirl-Sportscraft, who've refused to sign the union's Homework Code of Practice.

It sets out to protect outworkers by ensuring they have legal rights to a fair wage and reasonable working conditions. The ACTU says late on Friday Sportsgirl stores heard of today's planned union "shops of shame" protest and gave in to signing the code.
Company Managing Director, Frank Whitford, has been unvailable for comment.
Meanwhile, ACTU President, Jennie George, takes the campaign to Melbourne's exclusive Chaple Street and Toorak Road shops during lunchtime today.
FISCHER ADMITS PROBLEMS SELLING DROUGHT RELIEF RECORD
Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer has conceded the Federal Government is having trouble selling its record on drought relief to the bush.
But Mr Fischer says he stands by the decision of the Minister for Primary Industries, John Anderson, to revoke provisions for exceptional circumstances in 29 drought-affected shires.

The decision drew criticism at the Queensland National Party Conference in Brisbane over the weekend. Mr Fischer says if the Queensland Government comes up with evidence the policy should change, Mr Anderson will review the decision.
Mr Fischer says there is a "disconnect" in getting the message through.
"There are 16 decisions of the Government which not many people in the bush have even heard of, all of which are orientated to boosting income and the policy priority for the bush," he said.
TAX COMPLIANCE COSTS SMALL BUISINESS DEARLY
It's claimed tax administration is costing small business up to $7-billion dollars a year.
A survey by the Society of Certified Practising Accountants indicates that more than one third of small businesses spend more than five hours a week on tax administration.
The CPA's Small Business Index questioned 450 business in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney.
Executive Director, Michael McKenna, says the hidden costs of tax compliance confirm that Australia desperately needs a simpler tax system.
-- Reuters Sydney newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
